issues.legal_issue: A person seeking to uphold a transaction made by a pardanashin woman bears the burden of establishing that she executed it with a clear understanding of its nature.
material_facts: The woman and her mother-in-law were pardanashin and illiterate, and they placed confidence in the person who relied on the deed.
They put their thumb marks on a maintenance deed while believing it was a power of attorney.
The lower courts found that the deed had not been read or explained to them and that they had not understood its contents.
The person relying on the deed did not establish that the woman understood the nature of the transaction.
issues.conclusion: The burden rested on the person seeking to uphold the deed, and that burden was not discharged; the deed was not binding on the woman.
issues.legal_principle: A transaction with a pardanashin woman is not sustained merely by proving her physical execution of the document; it must also be established that it was her mental act, made with clear understanding and free will. The burden rests on the person relying on the transaction. The Court relied on Farid-Un-Nisa v. Mukhtar Ahmad (1925) L.R. 52 I.A. 342, Geresh Chunder Lahoree v. Mst. Bhuggobutty Debia (1870) 13 M.I.A. 419, and Kali Baksh v. Ram Gopal (1913) 41 I.A. 23.

rule.if: pardanashin_transaction and relying_person_seeks_enforcement and not informed_execution_proved

predicates.pardanashin_transaction: A document records a transaction entered into by a pardanashin woman.
predicates.relying_person_seeks_enforcement: A person seeks to uphold or enforce the transaction against the woman.
predicates.informed_execution_proved: The person relying on the transaction established that the woman executed it with a clear understanding of its nature.

issues.definition: When a person seeks to enforce a transaction against a pardanashin woman, the transaction is not binding if informed execution has not been proved.

issues.legal_issue: The burden of establishing a pardanashin woman's understanding of a transaction may be discharged through evidence other than proof that the document was explained to her.
material_facts: The dispute concerned whether the woman understood a deed she had marked with her thumb.
The Court considered the rule governing the burden of proof and stated that the explanation of the document is not the only way to establish understanding and voluntary execution.
issues.conclusion: The burden may be discharged by direct or circumstantial evidence showing that the document was the woman's free and intelligent act, even without proof that it was explained to her.
issues.legal_principle: The inquiry considers the evidence as a whole, including the woman's proved personality, the nature of the transaction, the circumstances of execution, and the parties' history. The Court relied on Farid-Un-Nisa v. Mukhtar Ahmad (1925) L.R. 52 I.A. 342 and Jagadish Chandra v. Debnath, A.I.R. 1940 P.C. 134.

predicates.pardanashin_transaction: A document records a transaction entered into by a pardanashin woman.
predicates.other_evidence_establishes_free_intellig: Direct or circumstantial evidence establishes that the woman freely and intelligently undertook the transaction.

issues.definition: For a transaction with a pardanashin woman, the burden may be discharged without proof of explanation if other evidence establishes her free and intelligent act.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court cannot use a second appeal to overturn concurrent factual findings supported by evidence when the lower courts applied the correct approach to the burden of proof.
material_facts: The trial court and the first appellate court both found that the woman had not understood the deed and that the person relying on it had not proved informed execution.
Those courts considered the evidence, including oral, documentary, and circumstantial evidence.
The High Court reversed the concurrent findings after placing the burden of proving fraud on the woman and reassessing the evidence.
The Supreme Court found that the lower courts had applied the correct burden of proof and that their factual findings were supported by evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not entitled to interfere with the concurrent findings in second appeal; its decree was set aside and the decree granting relief to the woman was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a second appeal does not permit interference merely because the High Court disagrees with findings of fact. Concurrent factual findings reached on the correct legal approach and supported by evidence are binding absent a permissible ground for interference.

rule.if: second_appeal and concurrent_factual_findings and findings_supported_by_evidence and lower_courts_used_correct_burden

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding before the High Court is a second appeal.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and the first appellate court reached the same factual findings.
predicates.findings_supported_by_evidence: The concurrent findings are supported by evidence considered by the lower courts.
predicates.lower_courts_used_correct_burden: The lower courts assessed the evidence using the legally applicable burden of proof.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, the High Court may not overturn concurrent factual findings when they are evidence-supported and the lower courts used the correct burden of proof.
